why: Sentence and citation both check out; the finding still fails on subsystem and on consequence. (1) The quoted sentence exists VERBATIM at w28.md:50, as a whole one-clause <div> with nothing after it that reverses the conclusion. (2) removal-circuit-breaker.ts:71 and :83-86 say exactly what was claimed. (3) But that module is the WRONG SUBSYSTEM. It implements the permissions.md root/home floor (S4) — the breaker that fires in EVERY mode including bypassPermissions, whose documented scope is precisely 'removals targeting the filesystem root or home directory' (permissions.md:63). Its call site, pre-tool-use.ts:1186-1200, cites exactly that. Declining to fire on an unresolvable target is the CORRECT reading of that page: the qualifier is part of the contract, and the module's own rationale at :34-37 explains that a breaker firing on every computed argument gets routed around and then protects nothing. The w28 line is about AUTO MODE's classifier, a different and looser mechanism. This is the sibling-subsystem false positive the repo guide names. (4) The CONSEQUENCE, verified separately, is false — auto mode DOES prompt. An `rm -rf $VAR` in auto mode: AUTO_RISKY_BASH_PATTERNS[0] (pre-tool-use.ts:1751) matches `\brm\b`, so isRiskyAutoBashCommand (:2055-2065) returns true and the call lands in the prompt band. The guardian is then consulted, and GUARDIAN_POLICY_PROMPT orders exactly the documented behaviour: ':177' — 'When evaluating destructive local filesystem actions, especially rm -rf, attempt a read-only inspection of the target path first'; ':178' — 'If important context is missing and cannot be verified, lean conservative'; ':190' — 'Emit unsure when you genuinely cannot reach a confident no_objection or deny — missing evidence you could not resolve ... unsure routes the decision to the human; it is the correct fail-closed choice under real uncertainty. NEVER emit no_objection to resolve doubt.' An unresolvable variable is precisely a target the read-only inspection cannot resolve. `unsure` maps to GuardianConsultOutcome { kind: 'ask' } (guardian-consult.ts:68, :75), and the module contract at :23-27 states that a missing port, a disabled setting, an open circuit, an `unsure` verdict or any judge failure 'all resolve to the band's existing ASK behavior — fail-closed to a human, never to auto-run.' So the prompt happens whether the guardian runs, is disabled, or errors. The finding dismissed guardian.ts:150/:177 as 'about inspecting a specific local path' while skipping :178 and :190, which are the two lines that carry the unresolved-target case. (5) Not one of the nine owner decisions in inert-worklist.md section 3 (checked; the nearest, #3 autoMode.classifyAllShell, is a different control and its band now exists at pre-tool-use.ts:2129+). Not a Nessy product difference either.
correctedState: Conformant. The fork prompts for an rm -rf whose target it cannot resolve, via auto mode's classifier band rather than via the root/home circuit breaker. `rm` matches AUTO_RISKY_BASH_PATTERNS[0] (pre-tool-use.ts:1751), so isRiskyAutoBashCommand routes every rm into auto mode's prompt band; the guardian judge is instructed to inspect the target path read-only first (guardian.ts:177), to lean conservative when context is missing and unverifiable (:178), and to emit `unsure` rather than no_objection under unresolved doubt (:190); `unsure` resolves to kind:'ask' (guardian-consult.ts:68,:75), and per that module's contract (:23-27) a missing port, disabled setting, open circuit, unsure verdict or judge failure all fall back to asking a human. removal-circuit-breaker.ts is a separate, stricter always-on floor for root/home removals in every mode including bypassPermissions; its exact-target-only rule is the documented permissions.md:63 scope, not a divergence.
